column1: Using knowledge graphs and behaviour trees for feedback-aware presentation agents
column2: Nils Axelsson; Gabriel Skantze
column4: Proceedings of the 20th ACM International Conference on Intelligent Virtual Agents (IVA 2020), ACM. DOI: 10.1145/3383652.3423884
column5: Medium–high within the KG+BT niche; Semantic Scholar surfaced 19 citations (checked Oct. 2026).
column7: A foundational direct-combination paper. It extends an earlier behavior-tree model of adaptive presentations so that presentation content is generated from a knowledge graph, specifically Wikidata, rather than from a fixed hand-authored script. The behavior tree controls presentation flow and reactions to listener feedback, while the knowledge graph provides entities and relations from which the presentation is assembled and whose communicated/grounded status can be tracked. The work is important because it gives a clean division of labor: the KG stores declarative content and semantic relations; the BT supplies reactive, inspectable interaction control. Relevance: direct use of both concepts in one running interactive-agent architecture.
column8: A presentation agent can become more scalable and feedback-aware by combining knowledge-graph-derived content with behavior-tree-based interaction control.
column9: The evaluation is tied to a presentation/dialogue setting and does not establish how well the architecture scales to open-ended physical robot tasks, noisy world models, or large dynamically changing KGs.
column10: It directly couples Wikidata-based presentation generation and grounding state with reactive behavior-tree execution.
column11: knowledge graph; behavior tree; behaviour tree; Wikidata; human-robot interaction; virtual agents; grounding; feedback; presentation generation
column12: The relevant presentation knowledge can be represented as entities and relations in a KG. Listener feedback can be mapped to a manageable set of interaction states that BT conditions/actions can use. The KG contains sufficiently accurate and relevant facts for the presentation domain. A reactive BT is an adequate controller for the temporal structure of the interaction.

column1: Behavior-Tree Embeddings for Robot Task-Level Knowledge
column2: Yue Cao; C. S. George Lee
column4: 2022 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), pp. 12074–12080. DOI: 10.1109/IROS47612.2022.9981774
column5: Medium; Google Scholar surfaced about 14 citations in the research pass (Oct. 2026).
column7: This paper is strongly relevant rather than a conventional external-KG-plus-BT architecture. It treats behavior trees themselves as structured robot task-level knowledge and learns vector embeddings intended to preserve useful similarities among tree-structured tasks. The representation supports retrieval, comparison, and reuse of task knowledge and later became useful as a retrieval mechanism in automatic BT-generation work. Conceptually, it bridges graph/representation-learning ideas and BT knowledge libraries: the 'knowledge graph' aspect is implicit in structured relational task knowledge rather than an explicit RDF/OWL or named KG.
column8: Robot task knowledge encoded as behavior trees can be embedded in a continuous representation that preserves task similarity well enough to support retrieval and reuse.
column9: Because it embeds BT structure rather than integrating a semantically explicit external knowledge graph, semantic interpretability and reasoning over typed world relations are limited compared with ontology/KG-based approaches.
column10: It introduces learned embeddings specifically for behavior-tree-structured robot task knowledge.
column11: behavior trees; task knowledge; graph embedding; representation learning; robot task retrieval; skill reuse; IROS
column12: BT structure carries enough information to characterize meaningful task similarity. Training examples span the structural patterns needed at retrieval time. A continuous embedding can preserve distinctions relevant to robot-task reuse. Structural similarity is useful even when environment semantics or execution context differ.

column2: Yuanhai Zhou; Shiqiang Zhu; Wei Song; Jianjun Gu; Jie Ren; Xiangming Xi; Tianlei Jin; Zonghao Mu

column7: A direct robotics paper connecting a domain knowledge graph to behavior-tree planning. The authors construct a specialized robot knowledge graph from heterogeneous robot/task information and use knowledge retrieval/reasoning to support task planning, with the resulting task represented/executed through behavior trees. The work makes explicit the idea that BT planning should not be isolated from semantic knowledge about objects, actions, and constraints. Reported examples include a graph containing task and ontology knowledge, demonstrating a practical knowledge-driven planning pipeline rather than only a conceptual architecture.

column9: The demonstrated knowledge base and task set are relatively small, so evidence for scalability, generalization to unseen domains, and robustness to incorrect or changing KG facts is limited.
column10: It uses a robot-domain knowledge graph as an explicit semantic substrate for behavior-tree-based task planning.

column1: KGGPT: Empowering Robots with OpenAI's ChatGPT and Knowledge Graph
column2: Zonghao Mu; Wenyu Zhao; Yue Yin; Xiangming Xi; Wei Song; Jianjun Gu; Shiqiang Zhu
column4: International Conference on Intelligent Robotics and Applications (ICIRA 2023), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer, pp. 340–351. DOI: 10.1007/978-981-99-6495-6_29
column5: Medium; influential as an early KG+LLM+BT robotics architecture, but a reliable citation count was not surfaced in the research pass.
column7: KGGPT combines a robot knowledge graph with ChatGPT to generate robot task plans in behavior-tree form. The KG models robot skills, task rules, and environmental constraints; relevant graph knowledge is translated into a semantic description that grounds the language model before plan generation. The LLM then composes available skills into a BT, giving a more structured and executable result than unconstrained natural-language planning. In an office-service setting, the paper reports advantages over PDDL-based and ChatGPT-only baselines, making it an early example of graph-grounded generative BT synthesis.
column8: Grounding an LLM with structured robot knowledge from a KG enables more feasible and domain-consistent behavior-tree task plans than using the LLM alone.
column9: The approach still depends on an LLM whose outputs can be nondeterministic, while the experiments are too limited to establish safety or correctness guarantees under broad real-world variation.
column10: It injects KG-derived robot skills, rules, and constraints into ChatGPT and uses the grounded model to synthesize executable behavior trees.
column11: knowledge graph; ChatGPT; large language model; behavior tree; robot planning; task planning; grounding; ICIRA
column12: The KG contains the skills, rules, and constraints needed to make a task feasible. Relevant graph facts can be serialized into prompts without losing critical semantics. The LLM can reliably map those grounded descriptions into valid BT structures. Primitive robot skills exposed to the model execute as specified.

column1: SkiROS2: A Skill-Based Robot Control Platform for ROS
column2: Matthias Mayr; Francesco Rovida; Volker Krüger
column4: 2023 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), pp. 6273–6280. DOI: 10.1109/IROS55552.2023.10342216
column5: High for this niche; Google Scholar surfaced about 62 citations in the Oct. 2026 research pass.
column7: SkiROS2 is a skill-based ROS control platform in which semantic robot/world knowledge is represented through ontologies and an OWL/RDF world model, while behavior trees are used for reactive skill composition and execution. Although the paper often uses the terms 'ontology' and 'world model' rather than 'knowledge graph', the representation is explicitly graph-structured semantic knowledge and is therefore strongly relevant to KG+BT research. Preconditions, postconditions, and skill parameters are checked against this semantic model, while BT execution provides modularity, scheduling, and recovery. The platform is especially important from a software-engineering perspective because it operationalizes the combination in a reusable robotics framework rather than a single task demo.
column8: A skill-based robot platform can achieve reusable, explainable, and reactive task execution by coupling ontology/RDF-based world knowledge with behavior-tree skill orchestration.
column9: The semantic layer and skill library still require substantial engineering, and the paper does not demonstrate effortless scaling to very large open-world KGs or arbitrary unseen tasks.
column10: It integrates an ontology/RDF semantic world model and formal skill descriptions with BT-based execution in a general ROS platform.
column11: SkiROS2; ROS; behavior tree; ontology; RDF; OWL; semantic world model; robot skills; task execution
column12: Robot skills can be described through stable interfaces and semantic pre/postconditions. World state can be kept sufficiently synchronized with the RDF/OWL model. BT execution is suitable for coordinating modular skills and failures. The ontology captures the domain distinctions required for skill selection and validation.

The system uses multimodal user feedback to determine whether to continue, elaborate, or repair the presentation. column1: Conversational Artificial Intelligence with Neo4j and the Unreal Engine—Part 3
column2: Antonio Origlia
column4: Neo4j Developer Blog (technical article; not peer reviewed), 27 July 2023
column5: Low academic impact but useful technical/game-engine relevance; no scholarly citation count expected.
column7: A technical, non-peer-reviewed example showing how a Neo4j knowledge graph and Unreal Engine behavior tree can cooperate in conversational/game-like AI. In the described ANGMAR system, the BT queries Neo4j for a subgraph relevant to the user and uses that subgraph to assemble a Bayesian network for dialogue decisions; later BT branches decide whether to recommend an item or gather more information. Ontological part-of relations and graph paths also support explanations and argumentation. Relevance: one of the clearest publicly documented KG+BT examples in an Unreal Engine context, included to cover game AI/software-engineering practice.
column8: A graph-backed dialogue agent can use behavior trees as procedural control while dynamically extracting semantic subgraphs to support probabilistic decisions and explanations.
column9: As a developer-blog case study rather than a peer-reviewed experiment, it provides limited quantitative evidence, reproducibility detail, or comparison with alternative dialogue architectures.
column10: It demonstrates a concrete Neo4j-to-Unreal behavior-tree pipeline in which graph substructures are retrieved at runtime to construct downstream decision models.
column11: Neo4j; Unreal Engine; behavior tree; knowledge graph; game AI; conversational AI; Bayesian network; dialogue management
column12: The dialogue domain can be represented as a useful property graph. Relevant subgraphs can be retrieved quickly enough during interaction. The BT accurately reflects dialogue-control semantics. Bayesian decisions constructed from graph-derived information are suitable for the recommendation scenario.

This is strongly relevant to KG research because the ontology functions as a semantic graph that is queried to construct BT structure. It is best read as the initial version of the later, more complete journal framework.

column1: The NEMO co-pilot
column2: Stefania Costantini; Pierangelo Dell'Acqua; Giovanni De Gasperis; Francesco Gullo; Andrea Rafanelli
column4: CEUR Workshop Proceedings, Vol. 3762, Ital-IA 2024 thematic workshops, pp. 124–128 (workshop paper)
column5: Low; early workshop proposal, but a precursor to the later IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing architecture.
column7: NEMO proposes a human-AI co-pilot architecture whose central components are a user/environment model, a knowledge graph, and a behavior tree. Signals from the user, environment, and KG feed the BT; the BT can recommend or perform actions and incorporates an emotion-sensitive neural node; BT outputs plus user feedback are then used to update the KG. This creates a two-way KG↔BT loop rather than a one-directional 'KG informs controller' pipeline. Relevance: direct combination, focused on affective human-AI teaming rather than classical manipulation robotics.
column8: A co-pilot can provide more context- and emotion-aware assistance when semantic knowledge in a KG and action selection in a BT continuously update one another.

column12: User state and environment context can be represented meaningfully in the KG. Emotion estimates from sensors/neural models are reliable enough to influence actions. The BT can combine symbolic and neural inputs coherently. Feedback can be converted into graph updates without corrupting the knowledge model.

column1: Ontological framework for high-level task replanning for autonomous robotic systems
column2: Rodrigo Bernardo; João M. C. Sousa; Paulo J. S. Gonçalves
column4: Robotics and Autonomous Systems, Vol. 184, article 104861. DOI: 10.1016/j.robot.2024.104861
column5: Medium; peer-reviewed RAS article, still recent in 2026 and no stable citation count was surfaced.
column7: This paper proposes an ontology-based framework for high-level task replanning in autonomous robots and uses behavior trees for task execution. The semantic model provides explicit representations of actions, objects, conditions, and domain constraints that can be reasoned over when execution failures or state changes require replanning. It therefore occupies the same design space as KG+BT systems even though the authors use 'ontology' rather than 'knowledge graph'. The key contribution is the connection between semantic reasoning at the planning/replanning layer and a reactive BT execution layer.

column1: Interpreting Behaviors and Geometric Constraints as Knowledge Graphs for Robot Manipulation Control

column5: Medium potential; IROS paper but very recent; ResearchGate surfaced 0 citations during the research pass.
column7: This paper directly represents robot manipulation behavior and geometric constraints in a knowledge-graph form. Behavior-tree elements and geometric control relationships are interpreted as event-centric graph knowledge so that high-level behavior and low-level geometric constraints can be inspected and reasoned about in one semantic structure. The method is demonstrated on manipulation/visual-servoing settings, emphasizing interpretability and the ability to connect task semantics with controller constraints. It is unusual in the literature because the direction is partly BT→KG: behavior structures themselves become knowledge-graph content rather than the KG serving only as input to a BT generator.

column4: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), IEEE Xplore document 11127406

The authors build a specialized knowledge graph from heterogeneous robot information sources and use it to constrain or inform behavior-tree generation, so generated task structures reflect available skills, domain knowledge, and execution rules rather than unconstrained model output. The work sits squarely in the recent trend toward grounded generative robot planning: external structured knowledge is used to reduce invalid or semantically inconsistent BTs. Its importance is less in inventing either KGs or BTs than in treating heterogeneous robot knowledge as an explicit safety/correctness resource during automated BT construction.

column1: Behavior Trees vs Executable Ontologies: a Comparative Analysis of Robot Control Paradigms
column2: Alexander Boldachev
column4: arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.15274
column5: Low current citation impact; conceptually useful preprint because it directly contrasts BTs with executable semantic-graph control.
column7: This paper does not combine a separate KG with a BT in the standard pipeline; instead, it is a strongly relevant conceptual comparison. It contrasts imperative, tick-driven behavior trees with Executable Ontologies implemented in the boldsea framework, where an event-based semantic graph and dataflow rules directly drive execution. A mobile-manipulation example is used to argue that executable ontologies can provide reactivity and modularity while also supporting runtime model changes, temporal traceability, and a unified representation of data and logic. For KG+BT research, it is valuable as a critique of the usual architectural split between semantic world models and procedural BT controllers.

column9: The comparison is largely architectural and based on a limited practical example, so it does not yet show that executable ontologies outperform mature BT tooling on large safety-critical robot systems.
column10: It frames executable event-based semantic graphs as a direct alternative to behavior trees rather than merely a knowledge layer feeding them.

column12: Robot control semantics can be captured declaratively in an executable ontology. Event-driven propagation can provide sufficiently predictable real-time behavior. A semantic graph can remain understandable and maintainable as execution logic grows. The selected comparison task exposes the major architectural differences between the paradigms.

column1: Veritas: Structuring and verifying LLM knowledge for logically consistent behavior tree generation in LLM-based agents

column7: Veritas addresses the problem that LLM agents can generate behavior trees whose internal logic is inconsistent even when the natural-language plan sounds plausible. It structures knowledge used by the LLM and adds verification mechanisms around BT construction, aiming to turn loosely generated agent knowledge into logically coherent executable trees. It is included as strongly relevant to KG+BT research because the core problem is structured graph-like knowledge organization plus BT synthesis/verification, even though the surfaced publisher metadata emphasizes structured LLM knowledge rather than a conventional external RDF knowledge graph. Its emphasis on verification is important for the emerging generative-BT literature, where semantic grounding alone does not guarantee control-flow correctness.
column8: Structuring and formally checking the knowledge used by an LLM can substantially improve the logical consistency of automatically generated behavior trees.
column9: Its relevance to classical knowledge graphs is indirect compared with papers that explicitly use RDF/ontology/KG stores, and verification of tree logic does not by itself guarantee real-world safety or factual correctness.
column10: It couples structured LLM knowledge with an explicit verification stage targeted at logically consistent BT generation.

column1: Method for generating a behaviour tree for controlling a robot device
column2: Lavdim Halilaj; Anees Ul Mehdi; Niels Van Duijkeren; Stefan Schmid; Juergen Luettin; Ralph Lange
column4: Patent application US20250242491A1 / corresponding European family (Robert Bosch GmbH); technical patent literature, not peer reviewed
column5: Low academic citation impact but high technical relevance because the patent directly operationalizes a behavior-tree knowledge graph and graph embeddings.
column7: This patent describes generating robot behavior trees using a behavior-tree knowledge graph (BTKG) built from existing BTs plus background knowledge. Knowledge-graph embeddings are used to place graph elements in a latent space; a representation of a new task/prompt is compared with that space to select relevant graph content, which is then used to create or modify a BT and validate constraints. The document is not an academic paper, but it is one of the most explicit technical descriptions of BTs being stored, searched, and reused through KG machinery. It is included to capture industrial/software-engineering transfer of the research idea.
column8: Representing prior robot behavior trees and background knowledge as an embedded KG enables retrieval and adaptation of relevant behavior structures for new robot tasks.
column9: Patent disclosure establishes an implementation concept rather than peer-reviewed empirical evidence, so performance, robustness, and comparative advantage remain uncertain.
column10: It defines an explicit behavior-tree knowledge graph and uses KG embeddings to retrieve graph regions for new BT generation and modification.

column12: Existing BTs and background knowledge can be transformed into a coherent BTKG. Embedding similarity corresponds to useful behavioral/task similarity. Retrieved graph content can be adapted safely to a new task. Constraint validation is strong enough to reject materially invalid generated trees.
